2 · Paste the post copy

What does Cordova do with power it can't sell and can't ship out?

No transmission line leaves Cordova. 170 kilowatts of computing sits inside the Humpback Creek powerhouse. "The server was literally 20 feet from the generators," said Clay Koplin, CEO of Cordova Electric Cooperative. Koplin estimates 20 to 25 percent of Cordova's hydropower goes unused every year.

The Energy Department's July 22nd award list named a University of Alaska Fairbanks project and printed no amount. August 11th published $725,000. It funds software that forecasts demand and flags abnormal conditions, not the server. Alaska has over 200 remote microgrids.

The map with no line out, the twenty feet drawn true, and what the $725,000 buys.

What has to already exist in a village before AURORA-AI does anything there?

#AlaskaEnergy #Microgrids #GridResilience

3 · Post, then paste this as the FIRST comment (within a minute)

Cordova Electric Cooperative, its own about page. 1,566 customers, 18 megawatts, and no transmission line to other communities. https://www.cordovaelectric.com/about/

U.S. Department of Energy, the renaming of NREL to the National Laboratory of the Rockies, effective December 1st, 2025, so the partner list reads correctly. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/articles/energy-department-renames-nrel-national-lab-rockies

Editor's note

Carousel No.31 is the Cordova deck, nine slides descending from a measured 670 km frame to twenty feet of powerhouse floor and climbing back out. It ships as an explicit update to deck No.20, which recorded 150 kilowatts of computing at Humpback Creek. No page fetched this run carries that figure, so every string here reads 170 kilowatts, sourced to the National Laboratory of the Rockies on March 5th, 2026, and the ledger should record the correction rather than bury it. Three guards to hold before posting. The $293 million appears on no slide and appears in the first comment only as the size of the Request for Application, which is what the Department of Energy actually published, never as the sum of the 278 awards. The $725,000 is called consistent with the published Phase I band of $500,000 to $750,000 and is never asserted to be a Phase I award, because DOE has not confirmed the phase. Richard Wies is principal investigator and never a professor, and Cordova Electric Cooperative is a named partner and nothing more, since the claim that it supplies the project's operating data was killed. The caption is the room's winner byte for byte and it passed its lint, with no factual error to flag. One line to read twice, the caption puts the 170 kilowatts in the present tense against a March source, which is fair and is also the sentence a Cordova reader would test first. One number in this note was stale and is corrected here: the cover frame reads 670 km, not 720. The printed frame widths on the three map slides were typed constants until this run and are now derived from each slide's own projection at render time, which showed the old constants were wrong by 7 percent on 01 and 09 and 25 percent on 02.

Aftercare (this is where reach is won)

  • Post Tuesday to Thursday between 8 and 11 a.m. Alaska time, the strongest slots this page has measured. Drafts arrive daily, so holding one for the next good window costs nothing.
  • Paste the sources comment within 60 seconds of posting, before the first readers land. Every line carries its raw URL so the link survives the paste.
  • Reply to every comment in the first 90 minutes. The first 60 are where the ranking is decided.
  • Answer the closing question once in a reply of your own, so the thread has somewhere to go.
  • Check saves and comments at 48 hours and log both beside deck No.20, since this deck is the correction to it.
  • Never edit the post after it ships. A correction goes in a comment with the source URL under it.
